lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on UPI, Aadhaar and the state
lead.head: Paid by phone, priced in freedom

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 56

body: Amit Varma still pats his pocket for his wal­let be­fore he goes out. But since the hosts ar­rived for this shoot a few days ago, he has not taken it out once. He pays for ev­ery­thing by phone. {056-S01}

That wor­ries him. He and Ajay Shah have al­ways spo­ken of cash as free­dom[[x2]], and called de­mon­eti­sa­tion an at­tack on it. Yet, he ad­mit­ted, “it is super con­ve­nient to go any­where, just pay with your phone.”
Friends from abroad tell him India is get­ting one thing right: what some call DPI, dig­i­tal pub­lic in­fra­struc­ture, and oth­ers DPG, dig­i­tal pub­lic goods. Both terms, Varma said, are flawed.

The tech­nol­ogy, he granted, is amaz­ing at a nar­row level. But chap­ters 27 and 28 of *In Service of the Republic*, Shah’s book with Vijay Kelkar, con­vinced him that the whole logic of the ap­pa­ra­tus is flawed.
## Mind the words

Shah, “a Nazi on lan­guage”, began with terms. Economists de­fine a pub­lic good[[x1]] as non-rival and non-excludable, like clean air. Linux qual­i­fies. UPI, owned by one cor­po­ra­tion and closed even to non-banks as full par­tic­i­pants, does not. Nor does Aadhaar.
“No, just be­cause a gov­ern­ment mo­nop­oly does it, it doesn’t be­come a pub­lic good,” Shah said. {056-C01}

His larger tar­get was high mod­ernism, James C Scott’s name for the be­lief that pow­er­ful en­gi­neers and bu­reau­crats can de­sign so­ci­ety from on high. Real life, Shah said, is messier than a white­board.

UPI has no busi­ness model, so par­tic­i­pants never in­vest prop­erly. Payments fail: once, pay­ing a Delhi traf­fic fine, Shah saw one fail six times. Disputes go un­re­solved, and fraud hap­pens on a large scale.
Varma’s ob­jec­tion was sim­pler: mo­nop­oly, state-run or not. With ri­vals, a sys­tem must adapt or go bust. Shah added that the in­ter­net it­self won by fight­ing off a gov­ern­ment stan­dard.
“Single stan­dards are medi­ocrity,” he said. “Single stan­dards are the si­lence of a grave­yard.” {056-C05}
## The state that sees

The sec­ond worry is power. State leg­i­bil­ity, an­other of Scott’s terms, is the state’s abil­ity to see its peo­ple. States have abused such in­for­ma­tion again and again, Shah said, so every gain needs match­ing checks and bal­ances. {056-C07}
India is­sued its first Aadhaar num­ber in 2009 and still has no pri­vacy law. Shah and Kelkar call this pre­ma­ture state leg­i­bil­ity.

Defenders say the state could al­ways piece a pro­file to­gether from twenty data­bases. At Indian lev­els of state ca­pa­bil­ity, Shah replied, that was a real bar­rier, and a sin­gle num­ber re­moves it.
Why mind the state know­ing what Google knows? Varma’s an­swer was one word: con­sent. Shah’s was: “Google knows a lot about me, but Google does not have co­er­cive power on me.” {056-C10}
## What might have been

The al­ter­na­tive to UPI, Shah ar­gued, was never cash. Had India opened pay­ments to pri­vate and for­eign play­ers in the 1990s, Moore’s Law would have de­liv­ered any­way. Instead the Reserve Bank of India kept ri­vals out, PayPal among them.

As for the ide­al­ists who built these sys­tems, Shah does not doubt their mo­tives. But in pub­lic life, he said, an en­gi­neer must also be a bit of a philoso­pher. Varma, once dis­mis­sive of such in­sid­ers, now wants them in­side.
Shah’s part­ing shot was at the hype. “There is noth­ing about the Indian de­vel­op­ment cri­sis which re­ally will be ma­te­ri­ally moved by these tech­nolo­gies,” he said.

second.label: UPI fraud
second.head: Savvy, and still conned
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a clever friend’s loss to UPI fraud, and who protects users

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the friend who got conned

body: Ayush Patnaik, whom Ajay Shah calls an ex­tremely clever per­son, was de­frauded of 15,000 ru­pees through UPI. If even he could be conned, Shah asked, what hope for ev­ery­one else? {056-S03}

Over mil­lions of trans­ac­tions, Shah said, some pay­ments will go wrong. But UPI was de­signed top down, and no­body set­tled who takes re­spon­si­bil­ity or how con­sumer com­plaints are re­solved. When the payer says the money went and the payee says it never ar­rived, “there’s re­ally no way to get a re­course”.
On that gap, Shah said, a great wave of fraud has arisen, and the sys­tem is not ready for it. {#science} His ver­dict: “it’s a sci­ence project.”

quote.text: And if Ayush got conned out of 15,000 ru­pees, then imag­ine what hap­pens to den­tists and grand­moth­ers.

third.head: The PayPal India never had

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on PayPal and the RBI

body: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, Ajay Shah said, PayPal al­ready had what sounds like UPI to Indians: a pay­ment han­dle such as “Amit at PayPal”, with a back­end to send and re­ceive money.

Many Indian ex­porters were using it to get paid by cus­tomers abroad, in what Shah reck­oned were bil­lions of dol­lars. {#paypal} So PayPal asked the Reserve Bank of India to let it run do­mes­tic pay­ments too.
“And the Reserve Bank of India blocked that,” Shah said. {056-S05} Even today, he noted, UPI is open to banks only.

The cheers for UPI, he ar­gued, credit a state mo­nop­oly with gains that Moore’s Law would have brought through pri­vate com­pe­ti­tion any­way. {056-C11} There would have been five rival sys­tems, and mer­chants grum­bling over which they took. “We should grin and bear it,” Shah said.

p2.title: The case against DPI
p2.deck: Five objections to India’s digital public goods, set out by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

from1.head: Paid by phone, priced in freedom

quote.text: Anything that is the pri­vate prop­erty of one cor­po­ra­tion is not a pub­lic good.

photo.credit: Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India

box.title: Chapters 27 and 28
box.text: Amit Varma’s doubts about DPI were once about iso­lated things, like the co­er­cion in Aadhaar. Chapters 27 and 28 of *In Service of the Republic*[[x6]], by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah, showed him that the whole logic of the ap­pa­ra­tus is flawed. {056-R01}

sections.label: The first objection
sections.head: A monopoly by any other name
sections.caption: what a public good really is
body: If dif­fer­ent peo­ple start using words in their own strange ways, Ajay Shah warned, “we will get a tower of Babel.” {056-J09}
Amit Varma pushed back: lan­guage does evolve, and spon­ta­neous order is the best thing. But where spe­cific terms mean some­thing spe­cific, he agreed, they should not be messed up.
Economists in­vented the pub­lic good[[x7]], Shah said, and Paul Samuelson laid down the basic the­ory of clean air as one. {056-J10}

A pub­lic good is non-rival: your breath­ing clean air does not di­min­ish what is avail­able to me. It is non-excludable: it is not even in the­ory pos­si­ble to keep a new­born child from it. National se­cu­rity, law and order and the erad­i­ca­tion of small­pox[[x8]] fit the bill. So do Linux and OpenStreetMap.
## A fi­nite pipe

UPI does not. It is the prop­erty of one cor­po­ra­tion, a fi­nite pipe, and highly ex­clud­able: not even non-banks are al­lowed in as first-class par­tic­i­pants. Aadhaar is a gov­ern­ment mo­nop­oly. Governments are sup­posed to pro­vide pub­lic goods, Shah said, but a gov­ern­ment doing some­thing does not make it one. {056-C01}

Why the con­fu­sion? Shah saw “an el­e­ment of green­wash­ing”. Middle-class India cheers for the good words, and crit­i­cism starts to sound per­verse. “How can you crit­i­cise a pub­lic good? How can you crit­i­cise in­fra­struc­ture?” {056-C02}
~ Varma of­fered his own ex­am­ple of a di­luted term: “Oh, the mar­ket failed to give me a red shirt, it’s a mar­ket fail­ure.” {056-J04}

quote.text: Anything that is the pri­vate prop­erty of one cor­po­ra­tion is not a pub­lic good.

portraits.caption: Paul Samuelson
portraits.credit: Innovation & Business Architectures, Inc., CC BY 1.0

sections.label: The second objection
sections.head: Designed on a whiteboard
sections.caption: high modernism
body: High mod­ernism, Ajay Shah said[[x10]][[x9]], is the idea that pow­er­ful sci­en­tists, en­gi­neers, bu­reau­crats and politi­cians de­sign so­ci­ety and send the de­sign down from on high. The phrase ap­pears in James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, though it runs much be­fore the book. {056-R11}

Either we ac­cept it as help­less lem­mings, Shah said, or it is backed by co­er­cive power. Amit Varma noted how at­trac­tive the label sounds: “it’s mod­ernism, it’s high”. In truth, he said, it is co­er­cive power from the top down.
The real world, Shah said, is a com­pli­cated dance of asym­met­ric in­for­ma­tion, fraud, crime and con­sumers with prob­lems to solve. {056-C03}
## A sci­ence project

UPI, he said, has no busi­ness model, so par­tic­i­pants join as na­tion build­ing. A firm will put on a demo and rub shoul­ders at a rib­bon-cutting. It will not in­vest se­ri­ously with­out profit. {056-C04}

Monopoly makes it worse. Varma called it the key prob­lem, state or pri­vate: with ri­vals, a sys­tem adapts or goes bust. Shah went fur­ther. Linux has ten rival file sys­tems, and the United States has 13 or 14 rival com­pa­nies with their own elec­tronic health record sys­tems. {#ehr}
~ That squab­bling, Shah said, is where con­tin­u­ous im­prove­ment comes from, and pri­vate con­nec­tors bridge the gaps. A sin­gle stan­dard, by con­trast, is “the si­lence of a grave­yard”.

quote.text: The prob­lem with the high mod­ernist idea is it does not ad­e­quately grap­ple with the messi­ness of the real world.

portraits.caption: James C. Scott
portraits.credit: SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0

sections.label: The third objection
sections.head: The state can see you now
sections.caption: premature state legibility
body: Technology, Amit Varma said, in many ways does more for in­di­vid­ual lib­erty than any po­lit­i­cal move­ment. But the state can use it to op­press, and in India the bal­ance al­ready tilts its way: “we are ef­fec­tively sub­jects and not cit­i­zens.” {#subjects}

State leg­i­bil­ity, a term from James C Scott[[x12]], is the state’s abil­ity to see its peo­ple. States that amassed in­for­ma­tion, Ajay Shah said, have abused it again and again, so each gain in vis­i­bil­ity needs match­ing checks and bal­ances. {056-C07}
## Legible too soon

India is­sued its first Aadhaar num­ber in 2009[[x11]] and still has no pri­vacy law. {#aadhaar2009} Other coun­tries car­ried a com­mon-law tra­di­tion for­ward: a po­lice­man who can­not open my let­ter can­not read my email. India has nei­ther the tra­di­tion nor a mod­ern law.
Linking data­bases was al­ways pos­si­ble in prin­ci­ple. In prac­tice, at Indian lev­els of state ca­pa­bil­ity, it was hard, and a sin­gle num­ber re­moves that fric­tion. {056-C08}

Varma re­called that in the case against the ac­tivist Teesta Setalvad, the state went through her credit card bills, found she had once bought al­co­hol, and held a press con­fer­ence about it. {056-S07}

~ He noted that Rahul Matthan says the state could al­ways get such data by older means, and that Aadhaar does not re­veal your bank num­ber. Shah thinks that is not true; they left it for an­other day.

quote.text: every time the in­for­ma­tion in the hands of the state goes up, you need to com­men­su­rately in­crease the checks and bal­ances

sections.label: The fourth objection
sections.head: Give Moore his due
sections.caption: Moore’s Law and the monopoly
body: Amit Varma put the com­mon ob­jec­tion. It works, it is con­ve­nient, and the com­mon per­son says, “I have noth­ing to hide.” Why worry?

Ajay Shah’s an­swer began with the coun­ter­fac­tual. The al­ter­na­tive was never a world with­out elec­tronic pay­ments. Had India opened pay­ments to pri­vate and for­eign play­ers in the 1990s, Moore’s Law would have worked on pay­ments any­way.
Instead the Reserve Bank of India blocked them. So, Shah said, “we are at­tribut­ing the glory of Moore’s Law on elec­tronic pay­ments to UPI.” {056-C11}
## The magic of flight

His anal­ogy was Air India[[x13]]. Early flights felt mirac­u­lous: a plane, heav­ier than air, and “in thirty min­utes I had reached Bhuj.” {#bhuj} That was the great­ness of civil avi­a­tion, he said, not of a gov­ern­ment mo­nop­oly. Service im­proved once rival air­lines came in.
His sec­ond an­swer was about time. Many poli­cies feel great in the short run and turn out toxic. India cel­e­brated the Green Revolution, Shah said, but it was done by very bad means. {056-C12}
~ Varma pointed read­ers to the hosts’ agri­cul­ture episode, which shows how bad gov­ern­ment pol­icy is partly be­hind India’s di­a­betes epi­demic.

quote.text: Moore’s Law on elec­tronic pay­ments could have come to us by an­other chan­nel, which is a pri­vate com­pet­i­tive in­dus­try with mul­ti­ple ri­vals.

sections.label: The fifth objection
sections.head: No engineer is that bright
sections.caption: discovery, not design
body: The builders of these sys­tems, Amit Varma sug­gested, might say they can­not con­trol whether the state makes them mo­nop­o­lies or uses co­er­cion. They can only build the best sys­tem they can. Ajay Shah called this the “I’m a plumber” strain: blame the philoso­phers of India.

He does not doubt their mo­tives. They are ide­al­ists who stepped for­ward at a high per­sonal op­por­tu­nity cost to serve the coun­try. {#idealists} But in pub­lic life, Shah said, “you can no longer be an en­gi­neer. You have to be a bit of a philoso­pher.” {056-C13}
## No pointy heads

Consumer pro­tec­tion, fraud pre­ven­tion and the “hun­dreds of pages of man­u­als” should not be de­signed at all, Shah ar­gued. They evolve in a self-organising sys­tem, where every day peo­ple solve for their own self-interest.
No en­gi­neer, he said, is bright enough to de­sign the mod­ern world. Society needs dis­cov­ery, not de­sign, with­out “any pointy-headed guy at the top” plan­ning the Republic of India. {056-C06}

~ Varma wants Shah, al­ready a card-carrying en­gi­neer and econ­o­mist, to be­come a card-carrying po­lit­i­cal philoso­pher. If phi­los­o­phy has failed us, he said, ev­ery­one with a voice should jump into the breach.

quote.text: The mod­ern world is more com­plex than what any en­gi­neer can de­velop.

It is al­most im­pos­si­ble to en­vi­sion the emer­gence of the UK of the Renaissance and the Enlightenment com­ing about in China today. Because today the Chinese state is on top and it is using mod­ern tech­nol­ogy

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Four tales of networks, fines, freedom and the people inside the system

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the standard governments pushed, and lost
stories.head: How the internet routed X.25
body: Long be­fore India’s dig­i­tal pub­lic goods, Ajay Shah said, the same story played out in com­puter net­works. The world’s tele­com mo­nop­o­lies, many in the pub­lic sec­tor even in ad­vanced economies, got to­gether and de­signed a net­work­ing stan­dard called X.25.

Governments agreed to it and pri­vate equip­ment mak­ers fell into line. It was to be the great new global stan­dard. Shah found it “very rem­i­nis­cent of the top-down push that we see here in India”.

Something very dif­fer­ent hap­pened. The United States DARPA had con­tracted re­searchers, Vint Cerf among them, to build a stan­dard for bat­tle­field con­di­tions: ex­tremely ro­bust, able to han­dle fail­ure and reroute dy­nam­i­cally.
That, Shah noted, suits Himachal Pradesh, where the hosts were sit­ting. A line goes down, a line comes up, and TCP/IP shifts paths and finds a chan­nel through.

Bill Joy and oth­ers put TCP/IP[[x14]] in­side Unix. Academic com­puter sci­en­tists and hob­by­ists all over the world built BSD, which later turned into Linux. “So the en­tire in­ter­net rev­o­lu­tion came by fight­ing off a gov­ern­ment stan­dard,” Shah said. {056-S04}

TCP/IP also saw off Microsoft, then a large and im­por­tant com­puter com­pany with a stan­dard of its own, and Novell, with an­other. Two giant cor­po­ra­tions and one gov­ern­ment lost. “And the hack­ers and the hob­by­ists and the aca­demi­cians, they won.” {#won}

~ Why? Brain power and adap­ta­tion, Shah said: hun­dreds of minds all over the world, think­ing and re­think­ing. He pleaded with India’s pol­i­cy­mak­ers and bu­reau­crats, who he thinks “have failed to un­der­stand how en­gi­neer­ing hap­pens”.
stories.why: Standards wars, Shah ar­gued, are the sign of a healthy field, not a prob­lem to fix. The in­ter­net is the proof: a bot­tom-up stan­dard, built by many squab­bling minds, beat one backed by gov­ern­ments. {056-C05}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on how the internet beat X.25

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah, a Delhi policeman and a payment that stalled
stories.head: Fined in Delhi, failed six times
body: Ajay Shah was stopped by a po­lice­man in Delhi for going through a red light. The fine was not the trou­ble. Paying it was. {056-S02}
There was a catch. “The cop is say­ing I will not ac­cept the fine in cash. I will only ac­cept it in elec­tron­ics,” Shah said, “and the damn elec­tron­ics doesn’t work.”

Shah had per­fect in­ter­net con­nec­tiv­ity. Even so, the UPI trans­ac­tion failed six con­sec­u­tive times and went through only on the sev­enth, while he sat “grum­bling my heart off that this is the state of mod­ern India”. {#fail}

~ Failures are in­evitable over mil­lions of trans­ac­tions, Shah said. But UPI was de­signed top down, and no­body worked out who takes re­spon­si­bil­ity when one goes wrong. The user is com­pelled to use it and has nowhere to turn.
stories.why: A sys­tem pushed from the top, with the state forc­ing its use, leaves no­body on the hook when it fails. Designed sys­tems, Shah ar­gued, han­dle the mess of the real world poorly. {056-C03}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the fine that wouldn’t go through

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why Aadhaar is not like Google
stories.head: Google asks; Aadhaar doesn’t
body: Amit Varma ranted against Aadhaar and held out against tak­ing it for the long­est time. In the end there was no choice: to pay his taxes, he had to do the link­age, and he did. {#taxes}
People often asked him what he thought was a naive ques­tion. Why mind giv­ing your data to the gov­ern­ment, when you give it to pri­vate com­pa­nies like Google and Facebook any­way?
His an­swer was al­ways one word: con­sent. With a pri­vate com­pany there are terms of use, he said. He can delete his ac­count. Whatever he shares, he shares out of his own free will. {056-S06}

~ Ajay Shah added a sec­ond dis­tinc­tion. Google has no co­er­cive power, and the big tech firms he spreads his life across can­not sub­poena one an­other. {056-C10} The Indian state is un­ac­count­able and al­ready leaks data.

quote.text: It is a blow to my free­dom from the very en­tity which is sup­posed to pro­tect my freak­ing free­dom.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the one-word answer

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on outsiders, insiders and a litmus test
stories.head: The outsider who wants insiders in
body: Amit Varma has al­ways seen him­self as the quin­tes­sen­tial out­sider, an equal-opportunity of­fender to every party in power. Partly through con­ver­sa­tions with Ajay Shah, he came to see that he had some­times been un­nec­es­sar­ily harsh on in­sid­ers.

He still draws a hard line at de­mon­eti­sa­tion. It was, he wrote in the *Times of India*[[x15]] at the time, the largest as­sault on prop­erty rights in human his­tory. {#demon} Insiders who kept quiet failed a last­ing lit­mus test.

DPI is dif­fer­ent, he said. “If DPI is going to be built any­way, if Aadhaar and UPI are going to hap­pen any­way, I would rather have a Viral Shah and a Sanjay Jain and a Rahul Matthan in­side the sys­tem than out­side.” {056-S08}
~ He will keep grip­ing about co­er­cion and the panop­ti­con. But ten years ago he would have been dis­mis­sive. “Today I want them there.”
stories.why: Criticism from out­side and en­gage­ment from in­side can co­ex­ist, Varma sug­gested. The skill lies in telling which is­sues, like de­mon­eti­sa­tion, de­mand that in­sid­ers speak up, and which re­ward stay­ing in the room.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on insiders and outsiders

quiz.q: What two properties make something a public good, in the definition Ajay Shah used?
quiz.a: Non-rival and non-excludable: your use doesn’t re­duce mine, and no­body can be shut out.

quiz.q: How many times did Ajay Shah’s UPI payment of a Delhi traffic fine fail?
quiz.a: Six times in a row; it went through only on the sev­enth at­tempt.

quiz.q: Which networking standard, backed by governments and telecom monopolies, lost out to TCP/IP?
quiz.a: X.25, de­signed jointly by the world’s tele­com mo­nop­o­lies and pushed by gov­ern­ments.

quiz.q: What one word did Amit Varma give when asked why Aadhaar differs from Google?
quiz.a: Consent: with Google he ac­cepts terms and can leave; with Aadhaar he had no choice.

quiz.q: Which company, according to Ajay Shah, asked the RBI to let it run domestic payments?
quiz.a: PayPal, which al­ready of­fered han­dles like “Amit at PayPal”; the RBI re­fused it.

quiz.q: What does Ajay Shah’s book with Vijay Kelkar call India’s rapid rise in state visibility?
quiz.a: Premature state leg­i­bil­ity: the state sees more, with no match­ing checks and bal­ances.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 56. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India); Paul Samuelson (Innovation & Business Architectures, Inc., CC BY 1.0); Daron Acemoğlu (MeJudice, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic (chapters 27 and 28)
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
shelf.creator: Eric Raymond
shelf.why: Raymond’s ac­count of why Unix and open source work: the teem­ing, ar­gu­ing bazaar of un­paid vol­un­teers beats a few great peo­ple build­ing a cathe­dral.

shelf.title: Cathedral
shelf.creator: Raymond Carver
shelf.why: He calls it a mas­ter­piece that ‘just kinda blows me away’, and says it is free to read on­line.

shelf.title: The Collected Stories of Raymond Carver
shelf.creator: Raymond Carver
shelf.why: He ranks Carver among the great short-story writ­ers: min­i­mal, easy and el­e­gant, in some ways a suc­ces­sor to Ernest Hemingway.

shelf.title: Short Cuts
shelf.creator: Robert Altman
shelf.why: Amit was ex­cited be­cause its struc­ture echoed Altman’s Nashville.

shelf.title: Nashville
shelf.creator: Robert Altman
shelf.why: It is one of his favourite films of all time, and he calls it ‘just a masterpiece’.

shelf.title: True Names
shelf.creator: Vernor Vinge
shelf.why: It makes you think about iden­tity in a new way.

shelf.title: Vitalik Buterin’s writings on identity and political philosophy
shelf.creator: Vitalik Buterin
shelf.why: Ajay calls him a deep thinker at the global fron­tier of re­think­ing iden­tity.

shelf.title: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, with Ajay Shah as co-host
shelf.why: A three-way con­ver­sa­tion with Vitalik Buterin on pol­i­tics and iden­tity, the source of his in­sight that the core weak­ness of vot­ing sys­tems is how eas­ily peo­ple can be bribed, and of Ajay’s ar­gu­ment that cash’s anonymity pro­tects us from a sur­veil­lance so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: Rahul Matthan Seeks the Protocol (Episode 360 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Rahul Matthan makes the strong­est case that Aadhaar has pri­vacy built into its de­sign, the view Ajay chal­lenges.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: The Narrow Corridor
shelf.creator: Daron Acemoglu & James Robinson
shelf.why: Acemoglu and Robinson argue that lib­erty and pros­per­ity de­pend on a rare bal­ance be­tween state power and a so­ci­ety that pushes back, and that coun­tries can eas­ily fall out of that cor­ri­dor.

shelf.title: The UNIX Episode (Episode 32)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s deep dive into the bot­tom-up story of Unix and free soft­ware, built by peo­ple work­ing for decades with no promised re­ward.

shelf.title: Maps Are Magic (Episode 44)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ fuller dis­cus­sion of maps, which also gives Ajay’s ex­am­ple of a gen­uine dig­i­tal pub­lic good, in con­trast to UPI and Aadhaar.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: Insiders and Outsiders
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It sets out his changed view that in­sid­ers shap­ing a sys­tem can be as valu­able as out­siders crit­i­cis­ing it.

shelf.title: Narendra Modi takes a Great Leap Backwards
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit links Mao’s grand de­signs to de­mon­eti­sa­tion through one shared delu­sion, that a leader can re­design so­ci­ety to a mas­ter plan, and calls de­mon­eti­sa­tion the largest as­sault on prop­erty rights in human his­tory.

shelf.title: OSI: The Internet That Wasn’t
shelf.creator: Andrew Russell
shelf.why: Background his­tory of how a top-down net­work­ing stan­dard lost to the bot­tom-up in­ter­net.

shelf.title: How to make digital payments work
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s own case for how India’s pay­ments field should work, in line with his ar­gu­ment for open entry.

shelf.title: RBI’s proposal for a Public Credit Registry
shelf.creator: Prasanth Regy
shelf.why: A re­lated ex­am­ple of a state-run data­base pro­posed for fi­nance, rel­e­vant to the episode’s wor­ries about state leg­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: The collateral damage of regulatory roulette
shelf.creator: Vivek Ananth
shelf.why: Further read­ing on how un­pre­dictable reg­u­la­tion causes dam­age, con­nected to Ajay’s point that reg­u­la­tion is the core flaw.

shelf.title: Data localisation in India: Questioning the means and ends
shelf.creator: Rishab Bailey & Smriti Parsheera
shelf.why: Further read­ing on state con­trol over data in India.

shelf.title: India’s Policy Responses to Big Tech
shelf.creator: Smriti Parsheera
shelf.why: Background on how Indian pol­icy treats big tech, which mat­ters for the Google-versus-state com­par­i­son in the episode.

shelf.title: Stack is the New Black?
shelf.creator: Smriti Parsheera
shelf.why: A crit­i­cal look at the ‘India Stack’ ap­proach to dig­i­tal in­fra­struc­ture.

shelf.title: Digital public infrastructure and public value
shelf.creator: David Eaves, Mariana Mazzucato & Beatriz Vasconcellos
shelf.why: Another per­spec­tive on DPI, use­ful for set­ting against the episode’s cri­tique.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah on the Dangers of Digital Public Infrastructure (Episode 72 of Brave New World)
shelf.creator: Brave New World
shelf.why: Ajay on Vasant Dhar’s pod­cast, lay­ing out his fun­da­men­tal ob­jec­tion to India’s so-called ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic goods’: by the strict def­i­ni­tion they are gen­er­ally rival and ex­clud­able, so they are not pub­lic goods at all.

shelf.title: Exploring Digital Public Goods
shelf.why: A re­source on the dig­i­tal pub­lic goods idea whose ter­mi­nol­ogy the episode ques­tions.

laughs.text: When the crew calls ‘Amit rolling’ be­fore the take, Amit says: ‘it’s very easy to get a Bengali like me rolling be­cause an es­sen­tial con­di­tion for that is round­ness. And I have a lot of that. I’m try­ing to lose some of it.’
Amit on how tech­ni­cal terms get di­luted: ‘Oh, the mar­ket failed to give me a red shirt, it’s a mar­ket fail­ure.’
Amit jus­ti­fies wan­der­ing off to Raymond Carver and Robert Altman in an episode about DPI: ‘these are pay­ments for the soul.’
Tower of Babel: Ajay warns that if ev­ery­one uses tech­ni­cal words in their own way, ‘we will get a tower of Babel.’
Paul Samuelson, cred­ited by Ajay with the basic the­ory of clean air as a pub­lic good, which he calls ‘one of the great mile­stones in his­tory.’
